checkpoints.title: Choosing the Scope Verified by Testing
checkpoints.prompt: A developer observes a failure that occurs only when the order API is connected to an HTTP client, database, and authentication service. Select one type of test that verifies this integration.

choices.text: Integration test
choices.explanation: It verifies connections among multiple components or external boundaries.

choices.text: Unit test
choices.explanation: It targets the local rules of a single function.

choices.text: Static analysis (lint) only
choices.explanation: It does not verify connections at runtime.

choices.text: Screen-image comparison only
choices.explanation: It cannot verify the HTTP, database, and authentication boundaries.

learning.reason: It verifies connections among multiple components or external boundaries.

checkpoints.title: Set inputs, assumptions, and expected values so the test can be reproduced
checkpoints.prompt: A developer regression-tests a calculation in which the tax rate changes based on the effective date. Select two combinations that improve reproducibility.

choices.text: Fix the effective date, tax rate, amount, and expected value
choices.explanation: You can rerun it under the same conditions.

choices.text: Fix the mapping table between the tax rate and expected value for each date and time
choices.explanation: You can reproduce time-dependent branches.

choices.text: Generate the expected value from the execution result
choices.explanation: Errors cannot be detected.

choices.text: Do not save the inputs and expected values when a failure occurs
choices.explanation: Information needed for reproduction is lost.

learning.reason: You can rerun it under the same conditions. You can reproduce time-dependent branches.

checkpoints.title: Use test results as conditions for proceeding to the next step
checkpoints.prompt: A release manager decides whether to deploy to production using quality gates that include required type checks and integration tests. Select two stop conditions.

choices.text: One required integration test fails
choices.explanation: Failure of a required test is a stop condition.

choices.text: The wording of an optional description differs slightly
choices.explanation: This is not an explicitly stated required condition.

choices.text: A required type check fails, and the report is saved
choices.explanation: Stop after confirming the failure and the evidence.

choices.text: Skip artifact identification because all tests passed
choices.explanation: Test success and artifact identity are separate conditions.

learning.reason: Failure of a required test is a stop condition. Stop after confirming the failure and the evidence.

checkpoints.title: Reproduce failures so the same defect can be detected
checkpoints.prompt: A developer confirmed in production a defect that produces an incorrect billing amount at an input boundary value. After fixing it, select one procedure for detecting recurrence of the same defect.

choices.text: Delete the logs and rewrite all the code
choices.explanation: This loses evidence and verifiability.

choices.text: Fix the minimum input and add a regression test after correcting the cause
choices.explanation: You can detect recurrence by reproducing, fixing, and then locking it in with a regression test.

choices.text: Report that it has been fixed without adding a test
choices.explanation: Recurrence under the same conditions cannot be detected.

choices.text: Mock all external boundaries
choices.explanation: This hides actual integration problems.

learning.reason: You can detect recurrence by reproducing, fixing, and then locking it in with a regression test.

choices.text: Unit tests verify local rules, integration tests verify service boundaries, and E2E tests verify user journeys.
choices.explanation: This is the correct explanation corresponding to the scopes distinguished in the prompt.

choices.text: Integration tests verify only users’ screen interactions.
choices.explanation: A sequence of user journeys from the screen is the scope of E2E tests, while integration tests verify boundaries such as APIs and databases.

choices.text: If unit tests pass, authentication and data formats between services have also been verified.
choices.explanation: Unit tests alone cannot verify actual service boundaries.

finalQuestions.prompt: A developer uses unit, integration, and E2E tests appropriately to verify the quality of an order API. Select one correct explanation.
finalQuestions.title: Define test granularity

choices.text: Verify the discount-calculation rules with unit tests.
choices.explanation: Checking local rules within a small scope makes it easier to narrow down the cause.

choices.text: Delete the integration test with the payment API to investigate the cause faster.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Removing service-boundary checks prevents problems occurring in the payment integration from being detected.

choices.text: Verify the data formats of the order API and payment API with an integration test.
choices.explanation: This allows failures at the service boundary to be investigated separately from the E2E test.

finalQuestions.prompt: A developer narrows down the cause of a failed E2E test for completed purchases. Select one incorrect response.
finalQuestions.title: Diagnosing E2E Failures

choices.text: Unit-test the discount-calculation rules with fixed inputs.
choices.explanation: Local rules can be checked quickly with unit tests.

choices.text: Verify the discount-calculation rules only by checking whether an order can be placed from the screen.
choices.explanation: Even if one purchase path succeeds, you cannot conclude that all discount conditions and boundary values are correct.

choices.text: Delete the E2E test from login through purchase completion and replace it with unit tests only.
choices.explanation: Unit tests alone cannot verify the user journey.

choices.text: Run an E2E test from login through purchase completion.
choices.explanation: This verifies an important path close to the user experience.

choices.text: Investigate every failure only by rerunning the E2E test.
choices.explanation: An E2E test with a broad cause range alone makes it harder to narrow down mismatches in local rules or service boundaries.

finalQuestions.prompt: Before release, the order-service development team verifies the discount-calculation rules and that users can log in and complete a purchase. Select two tests appropriate for these respective checks.
finalQuestions.title: Order-Path Test Design

choices.text: Explicitly specify the inputs, prerequisites, expected values, and execution conditions.
choices.explanation: This is a correct design required to rerun the test under the same conditions.

choices.text: Fix or record variations in time, random numbers, and external responses.
choices.explanation: Controlling or recording factors that change the result is correct test design.

choices.text: Determine the expected value from the actual result each time the test runs.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Creating the expected value from the actual result risks treating a defect as the correct result.

choices.text: Delete failed inputs and actual results to speed up the investigation.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Inputs and actual results from failures should be saved as evidence for reproduction and root-cause investigation.

choices.text: Test boundary values and abnormal responses as separate cases.
choices.explanation: This is a correct design that explicitly verifies specification branches.

finalQuestions.prompt: A test engineer designs tests so that order calculations can be verified under the same conditions even after changes. Select two incorrect items.
finalQuestions.title: Reproducible Tests

choices.text: Save the tax-inclusive amount after execution as the expected value for the next run.
choices.explanation: If the expected value is created from the actual result, calculation defects cannot be detected.

choices.text: Fix the effective date and time, tax rate, tax-exclusive amount, and expected tax-inclusive amount from the specification.
choices.explanation: Fixing the time-dependent inputs and expected value in advance allows the test to be rerun under the same conditions.

choices.text: Combine the boundary-date-and-time case with the normal-value cases and check only one case.
choices.explanation: The boundary where the tax rate changes must be checked as a separate case.

choices.text: Do not record the input and actual result when a failure occurs; update only the time and rerun the test.
choices.explanation: This loses the evidence needed to reproduce the conditions and investigate the cause.

finalQuestions.prompt: A developer is validating order calculations that include the date and time when the tax rate changes. Choose one correct way to make the test reproducible.
finalQuestions.title: Testing a Tax Rate Change

choices.text: Isolate the test data and save the input, actual result, commit, and test environment when a failure occurs.
choices.explanation: This prevents contamination from other runs and allows the same failure conditions to be investigated.

choices.text: Replace the delivery API’s actual authentication and data format with unit-test mocks only.
choices.explanation: This cannot verify the actual service boundary, which is the purpose of an integration test.

choices.text: Every time the test fails, adjust the expected value to match the delivery API’s actual response.
choices.explanation: Matching the expected value to the actual result prevents contract violations from being detected.

choices.text: Use shared test data as is and omit cleanup after a failure.
choices.explanation: Other runs may change the data, causing accidental passes or failures.

choices.text: Design setup, execution, and cleanup, and compare the expected value at the actual boundary.
choices.explanation: This keeps the test environment and evidence reusable while validating the actual boundary.

finalQuestions.prompt: A test engineer is investigating intermittent failures in an integration test connecting an order service and a delivery API. Choose two correct approaches for reproducible investigation and validation.
finalQuestions.title: Rerunning Tests Across an External Boundary

choices.text: Do not deploy changes that fail to meet the required tests and passing criteria to the next environment.
choices.explanation: This is the correct role of a quality gate.

choices.text: Allow the quality gate to pass based solely on the fact that the tests were run, regardless of the results.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. The decision is based on the results and thresholds of the required tests, not on whether they were run.

choices.text: A quality gate should include the stopping condition for failures and the location where the audit trail is stored.
choices.explanation: This is the correct design for reproducing stoppage and investigation.

finalQuestions.prompt: The release manager decides whether to deploy to production based on the results from the validation environment. Select one incorrect statement about quality gates.
finalQuestions.title: Defining quality gates

choices.text: Fail the quality gate, stop deployment to the next environment, and save the CodeBuild report.
choices.explanation: When required checks fail and thresholds are not met, the correct response is to stop subsequent stages and preserve the evidence.

choices.text: Lower the coverage threshold only this time to meet the release schedule.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Lowering the standard to match the result defeats the purpose of the quality gate.

choices.text: Inspect the test reports specified under reports in the CodeBuild buildspec file, and confirm the target commit and execution environment.
choices.explanation: Associating the reports with the execution conditions makes it possible to investigate failure rates and cause trends.

choices.text: Delete the failed report and use only a rerun as evidence of success.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Deleting the failure report removes the basis for investigating the cause and validating the rerun.

choices.text: After fixing the cause, rerun the tests under the same required conditions.
choices.explanation: Maintaining the defined conditions makes the decision reproducible.

finalQuestions.prompt: A release manager detected a required integration test failure and insufficient coverage in CodeBuild. Select two actions that are incorrect before deploying to production.
finalQuestions.title: Operating CodeBuild Reports

choices.text: Document the required tests, coverage thresholds, and stopping conditions as quality gates.
choices.explanation: You can decide in advance what to measure and which results should stop the process.

choices.text: Store each build's test report with links to the commit and execution environment.
choices.explanation: Associating the results with the changes and environment makes it possible to investigate failure rates and trends.

choices.text: Use only the memory of the person who viewed the screen as evidence that the gate was passed.
choices.explanation: Without stored reports, the decision and investigation cannot be reproduced.

choices.text: For builds with a high failure rate, lower the threshold without checking the cause.
choices.explanation: Instead of adjusting the criteria to the results, investigate the cause and maintain the conditions.

choices.text: Delete failed required tests and make the decision based only on the remaining successes.
choices.explanation: Deleting required tests hides failures that the quality gates are supposed to detect.

finalQuestions.prompt: The release owner uses the results of multiple CodeBuild runs to decide whether to deploy the artifacts to the next environment. Select two correct practices.
finalQuestions.title: Evidence for Promotion Decisions

choices.text: Save no failure log and simply rerun all tests so that the cause can be determined.
choices.explanation: Without logs or reproduction conditions, it becomes harder to narrow down the cause.

choices.text: Ensure that even if the same input defect recurs, it can be detected using only manual memory.
choices.explanation: Recurrence detection cannot be left to human memory.

choices.text: Add the input and expected value that confirmed the fix to the CI required tests, and automatically detect recurrence under the same conditions.
choices.explanation: Adding the input that reproduced the failure to checks run for every change makes it possible to find the defect if it returns.

finalQuestions.prompt: A developer fixed a defect that produced an incorrect billing amount for a particular input. Select one purpose of retaining the smallest failing input and expected value as a regression test.
finalQuestions.title: Purpose of Regression Tests

choices.text: Record the first mismatch, inputs, actual results, logs, and the change commit.
choices.explanation: This is the correct starting point for reproducing the same failure and narrowing down the layer causing it.

choices.text: Reduce it to the smallest failing case and investigate the layer where the expected and actual results first diverge.
choices.explanation: This is the correct response for isolating the cause without expanding the scope of the change.

choices.text: After fixing the cause, add the same conditions to a regression test.
choices.explanation: This is the correct response for ensuring that the same defect can be detected by future quality gates.

choices.text: Without confirming the cause, delete the failed test so that the pipeline passes.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Deleting the test hides the defect and prevents its recurrence from being detected.

finalQuestions.prompt: A developer confirmed a test failure in the order API during CI. As the first response to investigate the cause, select one incorrect action.
finalQuestions.title: Handling Failure Evidence

choices.text: Separate the test environments and, even when sharing an external database, use different records for each test.
choices.explanation: Even if the test environments are separated, tests can modify the same rows when they use the same external database. Separating the data used by each test prevents interference.

choices.text: Share the same delivery-address record across all tests and rely on the execution order.
choices.explanation: This harms reproducibility. When different tests modify the same data, accidental passes or failures can occur.

choices.text: Skip cleanup after a failure and leave intermediate data for the next run.
choices.explanation: This harms reproducibility. The remaining data changes the conditions of the next run.

choices.text: Include setup, execution, cleanup, and result reporting in the test procedure.
choices.explanation: This is the correct design for rerunning the same conditions and preserving evidence of the results.

choices.text: Save the inputs, test environment, and logs from failures and use them to investigate the cause.
choices.explanation: This is the correct response for preserving the reproduction conditions and using them in the next investigation and regression tests.

finalQuestions.prompt: A quality engineer runs integration tests and E2E tests in parallel that write to the same database, designing them so that individual tests can be reproduced when they fail. Select two incorrect actions for this requirement.

source.label: Running parallel tests in AWS CodeBuild

finalQuestions.title: Managing IT/E2E Side Effects

blocks.label: Overview
blocks.text: Learn how to distinguish unit, integration, and E2E tests and verify results under the same conditions.

blocks.label: Learning objective
blocks.text: Determine the test scope and reproduction conditions, and use test results to make release decisions and prevent defects from recurring.

blocks.label: Learning objectives
blocks.text: Distinguish the scope and roles of unit, integration, and E2E tests.

blocks.label: Learning objectives
blocks.text: Specify the conditions and expected values that affect the results so that the test results can be reproduced.

blocks.label: Learning objectives
blocks.text: Determine the inspections and pass criteria required to advance a change to the next stage.

blocks.label: Learning objectives
blocks.text: Collect evidence of failures so that the same defect can still be detected after the fix.

blocks.label: Choose the scope to verify with tests
blocks.text: With unit tests, for example, you verify the inputs and return value of a function that calculates tax. Because the processing scope is small, it is easier to narrow down the cause of a failure.

blocks.label: Choose the scope to verify with tests
blocks.text: Integration tests examine the boundaries where multiple components are connected. For example, they verify whether an order API can connect to a database and correctly save the required columns.

blocks.label: Choose the scope to verify with tests
blocks.text: End-to-end (E2E) tests verify the flow from a user-facing entry point through login, order entry, and order confirmation. Because they pass through multiple functions, they can find important defects, but you narrow down the cause by examining each process.

steps.label: Choose the scope to verify with tests

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: We changed the order screen and tax-calculation code. We will verify the tax amount, the order record, and the operation flow.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Using fixed inputs, examine the return value of the function that calculates the tax amount.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Verify the write and read from the order API to the database.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Place an order from the user interface and confirm that the order completion is displayed.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: When a problem occurs, you can narrow down whether it happened in the calculation, data integration, or user operation.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: Because the order completed successfully once, you can conclude that the boundary values for the tax calculation are also correct.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: The range of operations and inputs that passed is limited. Verify the boundary values for the tax calculation with unit tests, where inputs can be rearranged easily.

blocks.label: Takeaway
blocks.text: Separate test targets by calculation rules, integrations, and user actions.

blocks.label: Takeaway
blocks.text: Verify first within a scope where failures are easy to find.

blocks.label: Define the inputs, preconditions, and expected results so the test can be reproduced
blocks.text: To reproduce a test, clarify what to input, from what state to run it, and what should be returned. If the result changes based on the date and time or an external response, record the values and conditions used as well.

blocks.label: Define the inputs, preconditions, and expected results so the test can be reproduced
blocks.text: In unit tests, fixing the time and external responses lets you verify a specific rule with a small number of inputs. When examining an actual database connection, prepare a test environment that can connect and separate the data used by the test.

steps.label: Define the inputs, preconditions, and expected results so the test can be reproduced

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: We are testing order processing in which the tax rate switches at midnight. The specification causes the result to vary based on the time on the day of execution.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Fix the date and time, time zone, and expected tax-inclusive amount.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Prepare inputs corresponding to the moments immediately before and after the tax rate changes.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Verify that even when the same test is run at different times, it produces the same result for each set of fixed conditions.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: Another person in charge can investigate the failed input under the same conditions.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: It is enough to rerun a test that fails occasionally, even if the inputs are different each time.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: If the inputs or execution conditions differ, you cannot confirm the same phenomenon. Record the conditions at the time of failure and fix the inputs needed for reproduction.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: State the expected result and the factors that may vary.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: When multiple tests modify the same data, prevent their conditions from becoming mixed together.

blocks.label: Use test results as a condition for moving to the next step
blocks.text: Quality gates define what to test, the criteria for passing, and how to proceed to the next stage. For example, they can prevent production deployment from starting when an E2E test that checks login and ordering fails.

blocks.label: Use test results as a condition for moving to the next step
blocks.text: AWS CodeBuild test reports let you see which tests passed or failed. Keeping a record of execution results makes it easier to investigate which change introduced a defect.

steps.label: Use test results as a condition for moving to the next step

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: For a change to the order API, unit tests, integration tests, and E2E tests for order confirmation are all required.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Check the results of all required tests.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Stop the deployment because the E2E test for order confirmation failed.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: After reproducing and fixing the failure, make the artifact that passed the same test a candidate again.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: This prevents changes that affect users from reaching production while a failure remains.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: If test execution records exist, the quality gate can be passed even if some tests fail.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: Execution records are evidence for the decision. Verify which tests were made mandatory and which criteria were met.

blocks.label: Takeaway
blocks.text: Make decisions based on test results and pass criteria.

blocks.label: Takeaway
blocks.text: Record the tested artifact together with its results.

blocks.label: Reproduce failures so the same defect can be detected
blocks.text: When a test fails, first record where it differed from the expected result, the input, the changes that were run, and the logs. Narrow down the possible cause one at a time, such as the code, test data, or environment.

blocks.label: Reproduce failures so the same defect can be detected
blocks.text: After fixing the cause, keep a regression test that can reproduce the failed condition. Confirming that it fails before the fix and succeeds after the fix allows you to detect when the same defect returns.

steps.label: Reproduce failures so the same defect can be detected

blocks.label: Scenario
blocks.text: When the order time was close to the time when the tax rate changed, a defect occurred that shifted the billed amount because the effective date was off by one day. A quality specialist reproduces the defect.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Fix the time and time zone of the failed order.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Exclude other processing and find the smallest input that causes the same shift.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Check the result after the fix with that input and add it to the regression test.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: It can detect when the defect under the same conditions returns in a subsequent change.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: There is no reason to keep the input or test from when the failure occurred because the fix has been completed.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: If you keep the input and expected result and incorporate them into testing, you can find the same defect even if it occurs again after a later change.

blocks.label: Takeaway
blocks.text: Preserve the information needed for reproduction.

blocks.label: Takeaway
blocks.text: Test the regression using the minimum conditions that caused the failure.
